## Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

### How the phase ends (changed)

By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has broken ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt, though none of the general reserve has been wiped out. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and outside the held belt the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security it needs. Inside it the summer is not the historical one: about 330,000 hectares of rice land have been titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most of the districts the government holds, and in those districts the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's¹. Where the government does not hold the hamlets at night, nothing has changed except the promise.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

About 1,100 village posts are settled, two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the infrastructure has begun to leave the villages around the posts². The sea route to the coast is closed and the Cambodian route open, and the enemy's rear is on the U-2S's maps while his regiments under the canopy and his cadres in the hamlets are as hidden as before. The general reserve enters Phase II weakened but whole, and the Front enters it with between 10,000 and 30,000 of the Republic's carbines³. On Guam the B-52Js hold about 1,400 measured targets in the cell's folders and authority to strike none of them in the North.

Phung Hoang ends the phase with about 140 district centres open, every one behind a settled post, and a method that has reached above the hamlet in one district on the edge of Saigon and in a dozen in the Delta⁴. About 1,100 selected advisers are in the subsectors and battalions, speaking to their counterparts without interpreters; the rest of the field posts are still held on the old tour. The Front has begun to move its district committees out of the held belt, which costs it the villages' daily obedience and gains it the safety of the contested edge.

By the end of July 1965 the board has filled about 70 of the army's roughly 190 manoeuvre battalion commands and relieved its first nine commanders; the rest are still held by men the generals put there, and about a third of all battalions are still commanded by captains, because the army is short of majors and the career-course gate makes none faster⁵. The companies are led almost everywhere by the classes of 1957–63. The generals are the generals of 1963, and every one of them has learned that the board can be bargained with and cannot be ignored.

The Directorate ends the phase with its plants at about half their capacity and the domestic share four months old; about 5,000 PF radios, 6,000 hamlet radios and 600,000 dry cells have gone to the held belt, and the Front's mines in Long An have Go Vap batteries in them⁶. Route 1 on the coast has been reopened after the worst flood in memory, and the Front has an industrial working class in Bien Hoa to organise.

The army that enters Phase II has trained every private it has enlisted for eight years, and every territorial; it has kept about 2,000–3,000 of its best sergeants at the training centres to do it, in the two years it could least spare them, and the Muster Service has caught the centres that sold the course short. The general reserve was broken at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and came back from both with more of its men than on any course before this one; the battalions are noticeably steadier than history's, though the enemy still chooses where they fight⁷.

The NCO corps that enters Phase II has been schooled for its grades for eight years, regular and territorial alike, and about 1,300–2,500 of its best sergeants are teaching at Nha Trang, the division schools and the territorial centres, on top of the drill sergeants at Quang Trung⁸. The 4th Marine Battalion at Binh Gia and the 7th Airborne at Dong Xoai were broken and came back with more of their men than on either earlier course, because their sergeants took command when their officers fell. The enemy has the academy's leader's manual and has begun to teach its local forces the ARVN platoon's routine.

The combined command ends the phase as a channel, not yet a command. It survived Khanh's coup by passing every order through his office, and it learned in its first month that operational control means what the junta of the day allows. Seoul and Canberra have consented on conditions: a Korean countersignature on every order to a Korean formation, and an Australian casualty estimate sent to Canberra. The task force ends the phase about 1,100 strong, with one campaign that found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section from one notebook⁹. The Hoc Mon committee that STILL WATER drove out governs from Cu Chi, and the task force's III Corps task group has its name.

The North ends the phase without the fixed economy it began 1965 with. Its fuel is in drums, its power in village diesels, its bridges are pontoons by night, its fighters are in China, and four SA-2 battalions rotate among about twenty sites that the Js strike as they are built. About 300,000–400,000 of its people are already repairing and carrying full time, a year early, and the Politburo has held three divisions at home against a landing that is not coming¹⁰. The flow south is untouched, and the American decision of July is history's.

MACV-JSOC ends the phase eleven months old and Delta ten, with 31 raids in the Saigon belt and the upper Delta in its first quarter alone, nine of them reaching a cadre the file had listed, and one operator dead at a doorway in Can Giuoc. Its one finished operation is NIGHT HERON, which took six of the eleven men of the Long An province committee at a sampan mooring with the province finance section's ledgers, and cut the Front's collections in three districts to about a third of the previous year's by December¹¹. The partnered cordon has been tried twice and abandoned, because a Ranger company told the hamlet what was coming and the battalion had to be told the night before. The unit has learned the country and has not yet learned what it will learn in Dinh Tuong: that the men it hunts can simply move, and that the price of its arrival is paid in the enemy's walking time.

The night over the posts changed in this phase and the war did not change with it. From January 1964 sixty-four AC-130J Ghostriders flew over the South every night, and by the summer of 1965 the Front had stopped assaulting the posts within their net on clear nights, moved its attacks into the rain, onto the posts beyond the net and into the mortar and the mine, and begun to fight from inside the hamlets. Nam Dong and Dong Xoai cost fewer lives at night and the same by day¹².

### New: The restricted area over Trung Lap
*7 March 1965 · Trung Lap and Phu Hoa Dong, Hau Nghia Province · EV014-9*

*Initiative: allied*

The provision's first near-disaster was procedural and it is worth one event, because the procedure is most of what the new headquarters was for. On the night of 7 March 1965 an assault team raided a house at Trung Lap on a Hau Nghia file. MACV-JSOC's operations centre declared a restricted operating area of two kilometres' radius for four hours and passed it, as its standing procedure required, to the ARVN 25th Division, the province chief, the sector adviser and the combined command's III Corps centre¹¹. It did not reach the Popular Forces platoon at the post 1,400 metres away, because the sector's night net closed at 22:00 and the platoon, at a post outside the held belt whose platoons had carried their own PRC-10s since April 1964, had no radio of its own until the Go Vap sets arrived later that year¹³. The platoon heard helicopters and small-arms fire at 01:50 inside its own village, stood to, and its leader took a squad up the hamlet path toward the noise. Delta's team, coming out with a prisoner, identified the squad at about 120 metres through goggles and went flat in a ditch until it passed; nobody fired.

Vance changed the procedure within the week: from 15 March a restricted area was passed down to the platoon holding the ground or it was not declared, which in the first year cancelled eleven raids outright¹¹. The incident is the clearest statement in the record of what the headquarters' deconfliction duty costs and buys. It buys the lives of the men on both ends of a hamlet path. It costs eleven targets in a year, and it is the reason a provision that needs a secret needs a joint headquarters more than it needs another squadron.

## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### New: Operation STEADY COUNT
*6 Dec 1965 – 30 Apr 1966 · Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes; Routes 23, 911 and 912 south to Tchepone; the Laotian panhandle · EV003-3*

*Initiative: allied*
STEADY COUNT was the first dry season of the panhandle watch, and it was named for what it did best. On 6 December 1965, the day Tiger Hound opened its strikes in the southern panhandle, the Global Hawk orbit moved from the II Corps coast to a racetrack over the Mekong side of the Laotian panhandle west of Tchepone, outside the guns and beyond the reach of anything the North could fly. From 60,000 feet its radar watched the roads that Group 559 had cut through the Annamite Chain that year: Route 23 south from the Mu Gia pass, Routes 911 and 912 from Ban Karai, and the fords and truck parks along the Xe Bang Fai and the Xe Banghiang down to Tchepone and Route 9¹⁴. The northeast monsoon gave Laos its dry season, and low cloud lay on the passes most mornings in January; the radar saw through it.

The engagement ran through three headquarters, and its weakness was in the joints. A track of six or more vehicles moving south at night went from the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut to the 2nd Air Division's control centre, from 1 April the Seventh Air Force's, and to the airborne command post, which passed it to whatever was in the air: A-1E Skyraiders of the 602nd Air Commando Squadron, B-57Bs, F-100Ds and F-105Ds on armed reconnaissance, and from the first night the AC-130J Ghostriders of the 17th Air Commando Squadron from Ubon, which flew to the tracks themselves¹². Strikes in Laos needed the rules approved by Ambassador William Sullivan in Vientiane, which allowed armed reconnaissance on the motorable roads. Of about 1,900 tracks passed in the five months, aircraft reached about one in six within forty minutes, found and attacked about one in ten, and destroyed or damaged trucks in about one in twenty. The pilots claimed about 560 trucks destroyed; the cell's own count, from tracks that stopped and did not move again and from the U-2S's radar imagery the next day, was about 210. Nine US aircraft were lost over the panhandle in STEADY COUNT's sectors, most of them to 37mm guns that Group 559 moved to the passes from January; seven crewmen were killed or missing¹⁵. The drivers, porters and road troops killed are unknown, and any figure for them would be invented.

What the counts showed was the war's arithmetic. Southbound truck movements through Mu Gia rose from about 20 a night in December to about 120 a night at the peak in March, and the radar measured what came out at the southern end, on the roads toward Route 9 and the A Shau. On 12 April 1966, the day history's B-52s first struck the pass with unguided bombs, the Js of HARD CROSSING cut the crossings at its foot with GBU-31s. About twenty hours later the orbit watched the first trucks cross again, on a ford the engineers had reopened beside the broken bridges, and the next night's Js cut the ford¹³. By February the drivers had learned the orbit's habits: traffic fell by half on the nights when the aircraft was late on station and rose in the hours of its changeover, and the road troops began to trellis the open stretches with bamboo and living trees. MACV J-2 estimated, from the tracks, that about 70–90 tons a day reached the South through the panhandle at the dry season's peak, and that this was more than the forces in the South required from the North¹⁵. It was the first time any headquarters had counted the Trail rather than estimating it, and the count said that the bombing raised the toll on the transit without lowering what arrived.

## Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

### Changed: Commando Hunt begins
*15 Nov 1968 · The Laotian panhandle · EV000-55*

*Initiative: allied*

On 15 November, two weeks after the bombing of the North stopped, the Seventh Air Force opened Commando Hunt, a campaign against the Trail in southern Laos fought in seasonal phases: dry-season phases against the trucks moving south, wet-season phases against the roads. Aircraft freed from the North were moved to it. It was the first campaign built around Igloo White: sensors seeded along the roads reported to the Infiltration Surveillance Center at Nakhon Phanom, whose computers passed target coordinates to strike aircraft, and gunships, above all the AC-130 Spectre, hunted trucks at night¹⁶. In this war there was no Spectre: the gunships over the Trail were the AC-130J Ghostriders of the 16th and 17th Special Operations Squadrons, the Global Hawk's panhandle watch was the campaign's third sensor from its first night, and the Ghostriders were sent to radar tracks as well as to sensor activations¹⁵¹³.

The B-52Js and the coordinate cell were its fourth instrument. Historically Commando Hunt's interdiction points, the Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes and the Ban Laboy ford, were struck by B-52 boxes and fighter-bombers night after night to crater them¹⁶. Here they were cut with GBU-31s on measured coordinates, and the Xe Bang Fai and the Xe Kong below them were sown with Quickstrikes set for the steel pontoons the North had brought in since 1966. The tankers freed by the J's range refuelled the F-4s working the passes, which flew about a quarter more sorties a night over the panhandle than the historical force could keep in the air¹⁷. The interdiction points did not close. The enemy had spent two and a half years building a net with no single point of failure; at Ban Laboy the cell now counted fourteen fords and two underwater causeways, and on any night the J could cut the ones it had measured and the trucks crossed at the ones it had not¹⁸.

Phase I, to 20 April 1969, claimed 7,322 trucks destroyed at a cost of 56 allied aircraft to an estimated 600 anti-aircraft weapons. The truck counts were not believed by the CIA, which estimated the North's entire truck inventory at about 6,000¹⁶. Here they were not believed by this headquarters either. The radar counted the trucks entering the panhandle at Mu Gia and Ban Karai and leaving it toward the South on Routes 92 and 96, and by that measure Phase I destroyed or disabled about 2,600–3,200 trucks and reduced the tonnage reaching the South by about a sixth, not the third the claims implied. The J's crossings added little to that sixth, perhaps a fiftieth part of the flow, because the net they cut had been built to be cut¹⁸. MACV J-2 sent the figure to Washington in May 1969 beside the Air Force's, and from then on the two numbers travelled together¹⁵. Commando Hunt would run until March 1972, and the Trail would grow under it; this time the growth was counted.

The tankers freed by the J's range refuelled the F-4s working the passes, which flew about a quarter more sorties a night over the panhandle than the historical force could keep in the air¹⁷. The interdiction points did not close. The enemy had spent two and a half years building a net with no single point of failure; at Ban Laboy the cell now counted fourteen fords and two underwater causeways, and on any night the J could cut the ones it had measured and the trucks crossed at the ones it had not.
> 
> Phase I, to 20 April 1969, claimed 7,322 trucks destroyed at a cost of 56 allied aircraft to an estimated 600 anti-aircraft weapons. The truck counts were not believed by the CIA, which estimated the North's entire truck inventory at about 6,000¹⁶. Here they were not believed by this headquarters either. The radar counted the trucks entering the panhandle at Mu Gia and Ban Karai and leaving it toward the South on Routes 92 and 96, and by that measure Phase I destroyed or disabled about 2,600–3,200 trucks and reduced the tonnage reaching the South by about a sixth, not the third the claims implied. The J's crossings added little to that sixth, perhaps a fiftieth part of the flow, because the net they cut had been built to be cut¹⁸. MACV J-2 sent the figure to Washington in May 1969 beside the Air Force's, and from then on the two numbers travelled together¹⁵. Commando Hunt would run until March 1972, and the Trail would grow under it; this time the growth was counted.

## Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

### Overview (changed)

Phase IV is the war of the American withdrawal. US strength peaks at about 539,000 in the first half of 1969 and falls to 474,000 at the end of that year, 336,000 at the end of 1970 and 158,000 at the end of 1971. American deaths by hostile action fall with it, from about 9,414 in 1969 to 4,221 in 1970 and 1,380 in 1971¹⁹. The Republic of Vietnam's armed forces grow to replace them: from about 897,000 in 1969 to 968,000 in 1970 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72, the territorial Regional and Popular Forces growing fastest²⁰. The policy has a name, Vietnamization, and a premise: that the South, given equipment, time and American air power, can hold what the Americans leave.

The shape of the phase is a race between the withdrawal and the South's improvement, run while Hanoi rebuilds. In the countryside, the years 1969–71 are the best the government ever has. The VC, gutted by the 1968 offensives, return to protracted war on a reduced scale; pacification spreads under Phoenix and the territorial forces, into a countryside where the land programme of 1964 has already done most of its work (the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 does not happen, EV000-65); and by most indicators, including the ones the enemy cannot fake, the VC's hold on the population of the Delta and the coastal lowlands weakens. On the frontiers the war goes the other way. The North rebuilds its main forces, extends the Trail and its pipeline, and after Sihanouk's fall loses Sihanoukville but gains much of eastern Cambodia. The United States uses the time it has to strike the sanctuaries it had left alone, secretly from the air over Cambodia from March 1969, on the ground in Cambodia in May–June 1970, and through the ARVN alone in Laos in February–March 1971, and Congress closes the ground option behind each attempt.

At home the war's support is gone. The Moratorium, the Cambodian incursion and Kent State, and the publication of the Pentagon Papers mark a country that wants its army home, and an army in Vietnam, after 1969, that is itself coming apart under drugs, racial conflict and attacks on its own officers, waiting to leave a war it no longer expects to win. In Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh dies in September 1969; the collective leadership around Le Duan negotiates secretly with Kissinger and, after the ARVN's defeat in Laos in 1971, decides to try once more for victory by conventional invasion.

In this war the phase follows the same course on the frontiers and in Washington. In the countryside it starts further on. The land programme has nothing left to do by 1970 but the communal lands, and about 1,150,000 hectares are titled by the end of 1971. The Commission Against Corruption, which had outlived three governments behind the American lever, loses that lever as the Americans leave, and in July 1971 Thieu puts it under a presidential inspectorate after it opens an inquiry that reaches his own circle¹.

The police and the provinces end the phase as the Commission does, working below the palace and reaching no higher; the historical gap narrows as the Republic builds after 1968 what this war had from 1964.

The enemy's rear is counted through the whole phase. The Cambodian incursion goes in on a map five years in the making and finds the caches in days rather than weeks, though Washington still names COSVN as the objective; Commando Hunt's claims are checked every night against a radar count, and the claim that the trucks destroyed exceeded the trucks that existed never survives a season; and Lam Son 719 goes in with an honest estimate of what waits for it, and fails for the reasons it failed historically.

The bombers' precision reaches the Cambodian base areas in 1969 and has a season of targets there before COSVN's rear services own nothing in the open. Over the Trail it adds a point or two to what Commando Hunt costs the enemy. In Lam Son 719 it teaches I Corps to build its defence around American bombs that will soon go home.

Three provisions of 1964 change the phase at three points. The American battalions go home as they came, whole, so the withdrawals do not scatter short-timers through the units that stay; the breakdown of discipline comes on its historical course regardless. The national Phung Hoang file, built since 1964 to the standard of a warrant, is taken into the palace's service with the Board and the Directorate in 1970–71 and consolidated in one building in Saigon for the election. And Phoenix comes before Congress in 1971 with an audited count since 1965 that its critics do not dispute.

The officer reforms reach the limit their memorandum named: the American lever. As the aid conditions are dropped with Vietnamization, the palace makes the board's general-officer list advisory in January 1970, keeps the board for everything below colonel, and in December 1970 answers a petition of colonels of the classes of 1957–59 by moving about forty of the army's best regimental and battalion commanders to staff and schools. Lam Son 719 goes into Laos weeks later with new commanders in two of the 1st Division's regiments and an Airborne brigade, and fails for the historical reasons, which were decided at corps and in Saigon. The battalions themselves are the best-led the Republic ever had.

Under the withdrawal, the Republic's own plants close the loop that Vietnamization would otherwise have left open: the American equipment handed over in 1969–71 goes into rebuild works and a signal depot that have run since 1966, and by the end of 1971 the RVNAF makes about two-fifths of its small-arms cartridges, most of its batteries and all of its wire, filled and powered from abroad. In the Delta the subsector advisers hand the call for fire to Vietnamese guns on Vietnamese sets before they leave. And the Directorate of Defence Industry goes to the palace with the Board, the list, the file and the Commission, keeping its output and losing its honesty.

The schooled sergeant meets the drawdown in both armies. In the American units that stay longest, the sergeant who enforces standards is the man the worst soldiers resent and some of them try to kill, and the schooled sergeant holds more squads together than history's without stopping the decay. In the Republic the gate on NCO promotion is the first of the army's merit rules that the palace breaks, by the National Day decree of 1 November 1970, in the same months it takes the board and the Directorate⁸. The academy survives the advisers, because it was Vietnamese from the start.

In this war the home front of 1969–71 has no My Lai and a smaller draft. The Moratorium and the Mobilization of 1969 come on their dates without Hersh's story, and the Peers inquiry and the Calley trial do not happen. A quarter of the men the boards would have called have enlisted before their notices came, the boards send about 70,000 fewer notices in 1969 and about 40,000 fewer in 1970, and about one in four of the Army's draftees in the rifle companies of the drawdown chose to be there²¹. None of it changes the withdrawal's schedule, which Washington set in 1969 for its own reasons; it changes the bitterness of the years in which the schedule ran.

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1971 the United States has about 158,000 military personnel in Vietnam, its ground combat role is nearly over, and the last US combat divisions are leaving¹⁹. The RVNAF numbers more than a million men under arms, well equipped and, in the territorial forces, more present in the hamlets than ever before²⁰. In the countryside the VC remain weaker than at any time since 1960 and weaker in the Delta than on the historical course; the land programme of 1964 has finished its work, with about 1,150,000 hectares titled, and the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 was never needed. The Commission survives below the rank of minister and general and no longer above it¹. The gains are real, and the government measures them.

On the frontiers the balance is the reverse. The PAVN has rebuilt its main forces, extended the Trail, lost Sihanoukville and replaced it, and watched the ARVN's best divisions fail in Laos. The secret channel in Paris is deadlocked on Thieu's removal and on the PAVN's presence in the South. In Hanoi, after Lam Son 719, the Politburo has decided to stake the next year on a conventional invasion across the DMZ, from Laos into the Central Highlands and from Cambodia towards Saigon, timed to an American election year and to the near completion of the American withdrawal²². Phase V asks whether the South can stop it with American air power and no American ground troops.

The posts, the census and the district Special Branch sections stand under a palace that chooses the loyal among the competent; what the Republic keeps from 1964 is the chiefs' experience and four extra years of files².

The radar's ledger has made the interdiction debate honest and changed nothing it was about: the Trail is larger than ever, and the aircraft that count it will leave with the Americans¹⁵.

The ARVN's I Corps ends the phase believing, on the evidence of Lolo and Sophia, that a besieged base under American bombers holds. It is true, and it is the belief that will cost it most when the bombers go¹⁸.

Phung Hoang ends 1971 with an audited count of about 63,000 neutralized since 1965 and a national file of about 230,000 names in one building in Saigon, serving the President as well as the war. About 3,500 selected advisers remain, with the territorials and the province teams more than with the divisions; the American battalions have gone home whole and their discipline has decayed on its historical course⁴.

The board ends 1971 as the machinery of the army below colonel and nothing above it⁵. The battalions that went into Laos came out better than the operation did.

The RVNAF enters 1972 with a closed rebuild loop and a domestic share that covers about two-fifths of its small-arms cartridges, a third of its 105mm rounds and most of its batteries, under a Directorate the palace now runs⁶. The districts of the Delta call Vietnamese guns on Vietnamese sets. The base has not yet been tested by a year without American supply.

The NCO academy at Nha Trang ends 1971 Vietnamese, as it began, with its American advisers gone and its course whole; the gate on promotion, broken by decree, has been half restored by the training command⁸. The American NCO corps leaves schooled and spent.

The 81st Gunship Wing ends 1971 holding the night over about two-thirds of the posts the Ghostriders held, through cloud on the coast where they never could, and in Vietnamese; the posts beyond its reach are attacked more often as the Americans leave¹².

The RVNAF numbers more than a million men under arms, well equipped and, in the territorial forces, more present in the hamlets than ever before²⁰. In the countryside the VC remain weaker than at any time since 1960 and weaker in the Delta than on the historical course; the land programme of 1964 has finished its work, with about 1,150,000 hectares titled, and the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 was never needed. The Commission survives below the rank of minister and general and no longer above it¹. These gains are real, and they are measured mostly by indicators the government itself produces.

The question of Phase V is the one Vietnamization was built to answer: whether the South can stop a PAVN conventional offensive with American air power but without American ground troops.
>

>

>

>

>

The American NCO corps leaves Vietnam schooled and spent, its best sergeants among the dead of the fraggings as well as the fighting.

### Changed: Nixon takes office; Vietnamization
*20 Jan – Mar 1969 · Washington and Saigon · EV000-56*

*Initiative: allied*
Richard Nixon was inaugurated on 20 January 1969 with a promise to end the war with honour and no published plan to do it. His national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, commissioned a survey of the agencies' views of the war, which showed deep disagreement about almost everything except that the South could not yet stand alone. At a National Security Council meeting on 28 January the Secretary of Defense, Melvin Laird, proposed calling the policy "Vietnamizing" the war; its two parts were to strengthen the RVNAF to take over the fighting and to extend pacification. Henry Cabot Lodge replaced Harriman in Paris²³. Laird, who visited Saigon in March, pressed for withdrawals sooner and larger than the military wanted, and made "Vietnamization" the measure of the South's progress²⁴. The Improvement and Modernization programme behind it re-equipped the RVNAF from top to bottom: M16 rifles for the regulars and then the territorial forces, M60 machine guns, artillery, helicopters, aircraft, and the training base to use them. In this war the RVNAF had carried the M4A1 and the M249 since 1964, so the programme bought no new rifle: its small-arms lines replaced worn carbines and sights, bought M855A1 for the territorial expansion, and added M60s, and the money went to artillery, helicopters and aircraft¹³.

### Changed: Operation Menu
*18 Mar 1969 – 26 May 1970 · Base Areas 350, 351, 352, 353, 609 and 740, eastern Cambodia · EV000-58*

*Initiative: allied*

On the night of 18 March 1969, 60 B-52s took off from Guam on a mission ostensibly against targets in South Vietnam; 48 were diverted into Cambodia against Base Area 353 in the Fishhook, where COSVN was believed to be, and dropped about 2,400 tons that night. In this war the 48 were Js, and their unguided carpet was half as dense; about 1,600 tons fell in the boxes, and twelve of the aircraft carried 240 GBU-31s aimed at the coordinates the U-2S had measured over five years in the Fishhook: storage sheds, a vehicle park, a workshop with a generator, and the clearings where the Global Hawk had seen trucks unload by night. The campaign that followed, codenamed Breakfast, Lunch, Snack, Dinner, Supper and Dessert after the base areas it struck, flew about 3,800 B-52 sorties and dropped 108,823 tons until 26 May 1970. Here it dropped about 75,000 tons, a fifth of the sorties carrying JDAM against measured structures¹⁸. It was concealed by dual reporting: an overt channel ordered strikes near the border inside South Vietnam, while a back channel ordered the strikes in Cambodia, whose records were destroyed after each mission; neither the Secretary of the Air Force nor its chief of staff was told²⁵.

The measured structures died; the base areas did not. In the first six weeks of Breakfast and Lunch about 300 structures that the U-2S had photographed were destroyed, most of them sheds and workshops in clearings. By June COSVN's rear services had moved everything that mattered under the trees and underground, and the clearings were empty when the U-2S next imaged them; the J's precision had a season's targets and then none. The rear services cadres, by the account of a COSVN logistics officer who rallied in 1970, blamed spies in the base areas and searched for beacons in the forest; they found neither, and did the right thing anyway, which was to own nothing that stood in the open. COSVN itself, a mobile headquarters of about 2,400 people under the canopy, was never located and never struck, as it was not historically¹⁸.

Sihanouk, whose territory it was and whose government had tolerated the base areas and the supply line from Sihanoukville, did not protest publicly. The *New York Times* reported the bombing on 9 May 1969; Nixon ordered the leak traced, and the telephones of 13 officials and four journalists were tapped. Historically those wiretaps were the first of the abuses that led to Watergate; in this war there is no Watergate, the burglary of 1972 never happens, and the wiretaps of 1969 are never exposed by an investigation of it²¹. The bombing forced the PAVN and VC to disperse and camouflage their Cambodian bases, here a few months earlier and more completely, but did not stop their offensives, and its effect on the war in the South is disputed²⁵¹⁸.

### Changed: COSVN Resolution 9 and the death of Ho Chi Minh
*Jul – 2 Sep 1969 · COSVN headquarters and Hanoi · EV000-61*

*Initiative: enemy*
In July 1969 COSVN issued Resolution 9, which accepted that the 1968 offensives had not produced the uprising and directed a return to protracted war: small-unit and sapper attacks, economy of force, the rebuilding of the infrastructure, and a campaign against Vietnamization and pacification, while main forces were preserved in the sanctuaries. It was a decision taken in the light of losses and on the movement's own reading of its position, and it set the pattern of the enemy's war in the South until 1971. On 2 September 1969 Ho Chi Minh died in Hanoi. His testament called for the war to continue until the Americans had left and the country was reunified. Power passed to a collective leadership in which Le Duan, as First Secretary, was the strongest figure, with Le Duc Tho, Truong Chinh and Pham Van Dong. Ho's death did not change the policy; it removed the one figure whose authority stood above the factions, and left the militants who had planned Tet in charge.

In this war Resolution 9 is issued on the same date with the same direction. Its section on the countryside is different in one respect. On the historical course the Front could still campaign in 1969 against a government that had not given the peasants their land. Here the government had been titling since 1964, and the resolution's instruction to the Delta's party committees was to stop contesting the titles, to treat a titled hamlet the government held at night as lost for the present, and to concentrate cadres and the reduced tax effort on the hamlets the government held only by day. That was a realistic instruction and a costly admission: it surrendered the issue on which the Front had been built in the Delta, and it left the movement there with nothing to offer the peasant but reunification and the end of the American war¹.

The resolution's instruction on the infrastructure was the Front's admission of what the police had done to it. It told the same committees, and those of the provinces around Saigon, to stop keeping cadres resident in villages with settled police posts, to govern them by visiting cadres who slept elsewhere, and to put the movement's best security cadres into penetration of the Special Branch and of the provincial administration rather than into the villages. A movement that had lived among its people since 1960 now visited them, and visiting cadres taxed less, recruited less and governed less².

It was a decision taken in the light of losses and on the movement's own reading of its position, and it set the pattern of the enemy's war in the South until 1971. On 2 September 1969 Ho Chi Minh died in Hanoi. His testament called for the war to continue until the Americans had left and the country was reunified. Power passed to a collective leadership in which Le Duan, as First Secretary, was the strongest figure, with Le Duc Tho, Truong Chinh and Pham Van Dong. Ho's death did not change the policy; it removed the one figure whose authority stood above the factions, and left the militants who had planned Tet in charge.

### Changed: The Cambodian incursion
*29 Apr – 30 Jun 1970 · The Parrot's Beak and the Fishhook, eastern Cambodia · EV000-66*

*Initiative: allied*
On 29 April 1970 ARVN forces of III and IV Corps under Lieutenant General Do Cao Tri attacked into the Parrot's Beak west of Saigon, and on 1 May the US 1st Cavalry Division and 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment, with ARVN airborne units, attacked into the Fishhook north of it; the 25th and 4th Infantry Divisions followed²⁶. In this war the attack went in on a map. Five years of the Sihanoukville count and the U-2S's radar change detection had located the depots where the convoys stopped, the road net that joined them and the clearings they hid in, and the 1st Cavalry's brigades were landed on the largest of them on the first two days rather than finding them by chance. The great complex that the 1st Cavalry found on 4 May historically, and that the troops called "the City", was its objective on 1 May here¹⁵.

Nixon announced the incursion on television on 30 April as an attack on COSVN. MACV had told CINCPAC and the Joint Chiefs on 24 April that the U-2S had heard COSVN's transmitters move west and north out of the Fishhook toward Kratie from 19 March, and advised against naming it as an objective. The speech was written in Washington, and it named it¹⁵. COSVN had moved before the attack. The PAVN and VC mostly avoided battle, leaving rearguards, and withdrew westward²⁶.

In the base areas the allies found the logistics of the war in the South: about 22,900 individual and 2,500 crew-served weapons, 7,000–8,000 tons of rice, about 1,800 tons of ammunition, 431 vehicles and 55 tons of medical supplies. Here most of it was found in the first ten days rather than through May and June, and the total was larger by about a tenth, because the depots on the map were searched first and the time left over went to the ones that were not¹⁵. The allies claimed 11,369 PAVN and VC killed and 2,509 captured; I make no adjustment to those claims, which carry the usual inflation. US forces were out by 30 June; the ARVN stayed on²⁶.

On 4 May Ohio National Guardsmen shot dead four students at Kent State University, and protests closed hundreds of campuses. On 30 June the Senate passed the Cooper–Church amendment barring US ground forces from Cambodia. The incursion bought time: the loss of the caches and of Sihanoukville delayed the PAVN's recovery in III and IV Corps, and the southern half of the country was quieter for more than a year. It did not destroy the sanctuary. The PAVN rebuilt its supply routes, seized Attapeu and Saravane in Laos, opened a "Liberation Route" through northeastern Cambodia to the Mekong, and in 1972 would attack An Loc from Cambodia²⁶. The radar watched the Liberation Route being built from the summer of 1970, as it had watched Sihanoukville; it could not stop it either.

### New: The National Day decree and the gate
*1 Nov 1970 – 30 Jun 1971 · The Presidential Palace and the Joint General Staff, Saigon; the National NCO Academy at Dong De, Nha Trang; the corps and division headquarters · EV010-6*

*Initiative: allied*

The gate on NCO promotion was the first of the army's merit rules that the palace broke by decree, and it broke it for the soldiers' gratitude. On 1 November 1970, National Day, President Thieu promoted every enlisted man of the RVNAF one grade, regular and territorial, without exception for the courses, as the government had done on national occasions before (M010·S11). The decree came in the same months as the general-officer list's demotion to advice and the Directorate's capture, and it was judged in Saigon as they were, as a matter of the President's gift. It made about 40,000–60,000 men sergeants or senior sergeants without the course for the grade they now held⁸.

The training command, under Brigadier General Phan Van Huong and with Master Sergeant First Class Lam Quang Phuc's academy behind it, did not contest the stripes. It contested the next promotion: on 20 November it ruled, under the 1957 regulation the decree had not repealed, that no man promoted by the decree could be promoted again until he had passed the course for the grade the decree had given him, and it opened the academy's second shift to them. The Joint General Staff let the ruling stand because the corps commanders, who wanted the stripes for their men, did not care about the next board. By June 1971 about half the men the decree had made sergeants had passed their course, and the other half held a rank they had not been schooled for and could not rise beyond. The gate survived the palace as a Vietnamese rule, enforced by the training command and the boards below colonel, after the American lever behind the board, the Directorate and the Commission had lapsed. Of the institutions the palace took in 1970–71, the gate was the one whose damage was repaired within a year, because nobody in the palace wanted it and nobody in the army needed it gone⁸. The academy's last American advisers left Dong De in March 1971; Rourke's successor reported that the course was taught as he had found it.

### New: The Commission placed under the Inspectorate
*14 May – 9 Jul 1971 · Saigon · EV001-8*

*Initiative: neither*
On 14 May 1971 the Commission Against Corruption opened an inquiry into the sale of import licences for fertilizer and motor vehicles under the Commercial Import Program, which its auditors had traced through three Saigon firms to a relative of a member of the President's staff. It was the first inquiry in seven years to reach the presidential palace, and it reached it in the year Thieu stood for re-election. The American lever that had protected the Commission since 1964, the Aid Compliance Board's power to suspend counterpart funds to a named command, importer or province, had not been used since 1969: the Mission was managing a withdrawal, and Washington would not risk a quarrel with the government it was leaving over a licence case. Commissioner Khoa's second term, from January 1970, had been confirmed with the American co-chair's concurrence; his removal still required it²⁷¹.

Thieu did not remove him. On 9 July 1971 he issued a decree placing the Commission, the Special Court's prosecutors and the Pay and Muster Verification Service under a new Inspectorate General of the Presidency, with authority to approve or suspend any inquiry touching an official of the rank of minister, general officer or province chief and above. The licence inquiry was suspended the same day. The Deputy Chief of Mission protested in writing; the Embassy did not invoke the Board. Khoa stayed in office and the Commission's work below that rank went on: the musters, the pay at the parade, the land court cases and the Phoenix audits continued through 1971 at about their earlier rate. What ended was the reach upward that had convicted a general in 1967. An anti-corruption body that had survived seven years with a patron and an American lever lost the lever first, and the patron followed his own interest¹.

## Phase V — The Easter Offensive and Linebacker (Jan 1972 – Dec 1972)

### Changed: The Delta during the offensive
*Apr – Oct 1972 · Chuong Thien and Kien Giang provinces; the U Minh forest · EVMT01-2*

*Initiative: enemy*

When the 21st Division left the Delta in April 1972 to fight its way up Route 13 toward An Loc, the regiments the PAVN and the Front had kept in the U Minh forest came out against the outposts of Chuong Thien and Kien Giang. Historically this is where the offensive reached the Delta's countryside: dozens of posts lost, districts cut off, and the government's figures for its own security falling for the first time since 1968. In this war the posts were different. The Popular Forces platoons of Long My and Kien Thien districts had held their posts beside the police since 1964, with the land titled behind them, and the attacks of April and May fell on posts that held about nine attacks in ten²⁸. The Front's regiments therefore did what they did everywhere else in this war: they left the held posts alone and went for the Regional Force companies the province chiefs had been made to send north as convoy escorts for the 21st Division's resupply, and for the road.

Major Huynh Cong Tri, the district chief of Long My, a list chief since 1966, kept every one of his forty-one posts through the summer and lost the road to Vi Thanh for seven weeks. His monthly reports, which CORDS forwarded to the Joint General Staff in September as the model of a district under siege, say that the Front's tax collectors did not come into the hamlets inside the post line between April and October, and collected in the hamlets outside it at about twice their 1971 rate. The same was true across the western Delta. The held belt stayed held at night through the worst year since 1968, and the contested belt beyond it, which the offensive gave back to the Front for a season, was where the Front's tax take and recruitment recovered²⁹. By October the 21st Division was back and the roads were open.

This is the half of the Phase IV gain that survived 1972. The Front's infrastructure inside the post line did not return in 1972, because the offensive in the Delta came as regiments against the posts and not as cadres into the hamlets; and the files of the district centres, which the attacks never reached, are the files with which the IV Corps provinces opened the "war of the flags" in January 1973. Night control in the held belt and the Front's weakness there were still noticeably better than history's at the end of 1972; what returned to history was the contested belt, the coast where a division came, and the government's legitimacy, which was lost in Saigon.

### Changed: Loc Ninh and the siege of An Loc
*7 Apr – 18 Jun 1972 · Loc Ninh and An Loc, Binh Long Province, on Route 13 · EV000-76*

*Initiative: enemy*

On 5 April the 5th Division of the PAVN B-2 Front attacked Loc Ninh, on Route 13 near the Cambodian border, and overran it on the afternoon of 7 April; the 9th Division took the Quan Loi base camp that evening, and the 7th Division cut Route 13 south of An Loc at the Tau O bridge with its 141st, 165th and 209th Regiments. An Loc, the provincial capital 100 km north of Saigon, was cut off by 8 April. It was held by the ARVN 5th Division under Brigadier General Le Van Hung, with the 3rd and 81st Ranger Groups, the 1st Airborne Brigade lifted in after failing to break through at Tau O, and the Regional Forces, Popular Forces and People's Self-Defence Force of Binh Long Province, all under III Corps (Lieutenant General Nguyen Van Minh) and advised by the American regional assistance command under Major General James Hollingsworth³⁰.

From mid-April a Global Hawk stood over Binh Long and watched the roads out of Cambodia¹⁵. From 15 April it was given the town itself, every night, and Sorrell's detachment at Long Binh measured what it saw: the PAVN's gun positions in the rubber, the bunkers dug into the ruined streets on the town's northern edge, the tank harbours, and the trenches the 9th Division pushed toward the perimeter each night. The 9th Division assaulted on 13 April with tanks; in that first attack the defenders destroyed tanks with M72 LAWs at close range, and tank-killing teams were formed in every battalion. From 16 April cells of Js came over An Loc every two hours, each with thirty to forty GBU-38s aimed at positions measured that night, the nearest about 400 metres from Hung's lines; by early May the PAVN's guns fired from the rubber a few rounds at a time and moved, and the town's shelling, which historically reached thousands of rounds on the worst days, came at perhaps two-thirds of that weight. The town survived on airdrops, taken over by USAF C-130s on 19 April once anti-aircraft fire made helicopter landings impossible³⁰; the guns around the drop zone were measured and struck each night, and the airdrops of May landed inside the perimeter more often than they had in April¹⁸.

History's nights over the town belonged to AC-119 and AC-130E gunships³⁰. Neither exists in this war. The night shift over An Loc was flown by the AC-130J Ghostriders of the 17th Special Operations Squadron from Ubon, the last American gunships in the theater, and by the AC-130U Spooky IIs of the VNAF's 817th Squadron from Bien Hoa. They worked in the hours between the bomber cells, on the sapper teams at the wire, the digging parties at the trench heads and the mortar crews in the rubber, 50–200 metres from Hung's lines¹². When the SA-7 reached the rubber with the 9th Division in the last days of April, both squadrons climbed above 10,000 feet. The Ghostriders' turrets and the Spooky II's radar fire control still worked from there, as history's gunships' did not, but the slant range cost them the closest work at the wire on the worst nights. They changed no part of the siege's course. The cells broke the assault of 11–12 May; the gunships made the nights between the cells dearer for the besiegers. For the 817th it was the first battle against a PAVN division with its own air defence, and the lesson it took, that the wing could not hold a sky the enemy contested, was the one Thuong Duc confirmed in 1974¹³.

The decisive assault came on 11 May. Historically B-52s struck one mission every 55 minutes for 30 hours against it, with AC-119 and AC-130E gunships, A-37s and AH-1 Cobras. Here the assault's assembly was on the radar from the evening of 10 May, as tanks and trucks moved up to the rubber north and east of the town, and Hollingsworth's targeteers put the night's first cells on the assembly areas the radar showed¹⁵. The difference the J made was in the hours after the attack broke into the town. Historically the B-52 carpets could not fall on the PAVN units inside the northern part of An Loc without falling on the defenders; here the cell measured the buildings and bunkers the attackers had taken, and cells of Js put GBU-38s on them 300–400 metres from the ARVN line, one aimpoint to a bomb, through the morning of 12 May. The 9th Division's penetration in the north was destroyed by noon on 12 May, and the tanks that had come in with it burned in the streets¹⁸. The 21st Division fought up Route 13 from Lai Khe. The PAVN was driven from the town by 12 June and III Corps declared the siege over on 18 June³⁰³¹.

US estimates of PAVN losses are 10,000 killed and 15,000 wounded and 36 tanks; Vietnamese figures are about 2,000 killed and 5,000 wounded. I estimate that the GBU-38 cells added to the PAVN's losses perhaps a fifth beyond the historical, and that the 5th Division and its attached units lost perhaps a fifth fewer killed than the historical garrison, and I do not alter the reported figures, which already disagree by a factor of five. Brigadier General Richard Tallman, the deputy American commander, was mortally wounded by artillery on 9 July³⁰. An Loc lay in ruins. It became the symbol of an ARVN that could hold if the B-52s came; in this war, of an ARVN that could hold if the B-52s came, the Americans could see where to send them, and an American cell could turn what they saw into coordinates¹⁸.
